doc.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

chapter: The music business then and now
title: How record companies and lawyers have changed the business
summary: Labels box artists into categories, chase young unseasoned acts, and managers are replaced by lawyers; Levy cites a 40-page Nancy Wilson contract.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: They probably do. I don’t know. But that’s probably the situation with them too. Because they want to put you in a groove, in a certain category. And that goes with everything, with singers and musicians. You’re in a certain category and you can’t do anything different. They want you to stay right in that groove that they’ve got you locked into. And it’s difficult to break out. You almost have to be in a position where you say I’m not going to do another thing until I do what I want to do on this. Because no matter what your contract is. I learned that a long time ago. The contract deals and the record deals with the companies. It depends on what you’re selling. I don’t care what it says, if you’re selling records and you’re making money for the company then you can do anything you want to do you know. You can make your own deal no matter what your contract is. But if it’s just an ordinary thing, they you have to go along with what they think is best. And today’s market is terrible because the people who are in the record business who are the people who make the decisions, they have no concept of the music or what’s happening. All they want to know about is, as they say, the bottom line. And they’re looking for young people with no experience or very little experience, and they’ll put the money behind them to make something happen for them, and then after that they’ll get another batch.
As long as they as they can tell them what to do you mean?

Oh, yeah. They tell you exactly what to do. That’s what they want. And managers like myself, they don’t exist today with the upcoming people, because in most cases they are lawyers or accountants that do the managing. And they have no idea of what it’s about, but there’s so much legal stuff going on, as I call it “legalistic” — the legalese of the business, the way —

Oh, yeah, yeah. Oh yeah. A person like myself who is not a lawyer, and I know about contracts, I know enough about it, I’ve been it long enough that I can draft one and I know exactly what’s happening with it. But they won’t accept that. You have to be a lawyer. Because you can, the record company can be sued if the artist signs with them without having a lawyer represent them. So it’s gotten to that point, where, like everything else in this country, anything you do, you have to have a lawyer almost to do it. It’s like we make agreements say to do something like this for the school, and it gets to the point where this is unusual, just that you’ve got a simple form to sign.

Yes, one page, simple form to sign. Because normally oh, it’s just pages. I have a contract, a Nancy Wilson contract that has 40 pages on it, for Columbia Records. Forty pages. And it’s, it gives you one thing on page five and takes it away on page nine.
And then it’s got something right at the end that says “if we forgot to say anything in this contract” you know—don’t forget about that.
They’ve got it worded, and you’ve got to go through all of that stuff today. And it makes it a little difficult. But—
